en.g: a female given name from English [in turn from Latin, in turn from Ancient Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew], equivalent to English Annie
x: Annie kommer på besøk i morgen.
Annie is coming to visit tomorrow.

1000469.etyen:
Borrowed from English Annie (“female given name”), an English pet form of Ann and Anne. The name ultimately derives from Late Latin Anna (“female given name”), from Koine Greek Ἄννα (Ánna, “Anna”), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “Hannah; grace, favour”), from Biblical Hebrew חָנַן (ḥānan, “to be gracious, show favour”).
Compare Danish Annie and Swedish Annie (“female given name”).

1000725.etyen:
From nes (“headland, promontory”) + by (“farm, village, settlement”), literally “settlement at the headland”, referring to the headland where Nesseby Church stands. The second element reflects the older meaning of by, corresponding to býr (“farm, village”), rather than only its usual modern meaning “city”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Nesseby.

A Norwegian place name borne by several farms, villages and other localities

1004565.etyen:
From djup (“deep”) + vik (“bay, inlet”), literally “deep bay”. The place-name type continues Old Norse compounds formed from djúpr (“deep”) and vík (“bay, inlet”). As a surname, it is habitational, originating from one of several farms or localities named Djupvik. Doublet of Gjøvik, Dybvik, and Dybevik.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Djupvik (“place name and surname”), Swedish Djupvik (“place name”), Icelandic Djúpavík (“place name”) and Danish Dybvig (“place name and surname”).
